source.title: Three Factors Influencing Minima in SGD
source.authors: Stanislaw Jastrzebski; Zachary Kenton; Devansh Arpit; Nicolas Ballas; Asja Fischer; Yoshua Bengio; A. Storkey

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including appendices; no apparent truncation or garbling that prevents extraction.
record.tranche_reason: Experiments vary learning-rate-to-batch-size ratio and measure validation/test performance, Hessian geometry, and performance after fitting randomized-label training sets. These are conceptually relevant to V1 and V5, but do not reproduce the original studies' full methods.
record.gate_note: Own results include training and validation/test performance across noise-ratio conditions, Hessian measurements, and validation performance after memorizing randomized training labels. Figure 6 provides no numerical performance values in the supplied text; its described outcome is extractable as an explicit statement. Table 1 provides exact values for cyclical schedules.
record.test_reason: Own experiments test coexistence of label memorization and generalization on partially corrupted MNIST, and whether learning-rate scaling preserves held-out performance when batch size increases under matched epoch budgets. The study is not an original source listed for these versions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate. The authors conclude that learning rate, batch size, and gradient covariance influence SGD endpoints; learning-rate/batch-size ratio approximately controls dynamics and, under their covariance–Hessian assumptions, minimum width. Higher ratios correlate with wider endpoints and better generalization. Batch-size schedules can substitute for learning-rate schedules, but proportional scaling breaks down at sufficiently large learning rates or batch sizes.
record.recipe_differences: Uses SGD and varies learning-rate/batch-size noise, but focuses on noise-ratio schedules, Hessian geometry, and partial label randomization rather than the original claim's full random-label versus natural-label comparison or fixed-epoch large-batch comparisons.
record.method_sensitivity: Learning-rate-to-batch-size ratio; schedule type (discrete cyclic learning rate, discrete cyclic batch size, triangular cyclic learning rate, constant); momentum (0.0 versus 0.9); randomized-label fraction (25% versus 50%); scaling factor β and dataset size; sufficiently large β breaks the scaling approximation.

fits_no_version.finding: Cyclic schedules improve VGG11 test accuracy over the constant schedule, with discrete batch-size cycling performing similarly to learning-rate cycling.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cycling SGD noise through learning rate or batch size can improve held-out accuracy relative to a constant schedule.

fits_no_version.finding: Higher learning-rate/batch-size ratios correlate with smaller Hessian eigenvalues or norms and better held-out accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unscaled Hessian curvature correlates with held-out performance across these SGD settings. This does not test V7's magnitude-aware perturbation measure or generalization-gap ranking.

record.problems: The memorization experiment reports no exact validation-accuracy values in the supplied text, only a figure and a qualitative result. Its generalization-after-memorization result uses partially randomized labels, not fully random labels versus natural labels. Claims about width and generalization depend on stated approximations, including a relation between gradient covariance and Hessian; the authors note scaling breaks for sufficiently large β.
record.rows_left_out: No reported result rows omitted. Exact Figure 6 values are unavailable in the supplied text, so the paper's explicit qualitative description is recorded for each label-fraction and momentum condition without inventing numbers.

untested.parts: Complete randomization with chance-level held-out accuracy; a matched natural-label versus fully random-label comparison; the original image datasets, architectures, and absence of explicit regularization.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
Language models, workload-dependent batch-size thresholds, longer-training recovery, warmup, and controlled normalization or regularization changes.
Magnitude-scaled weight perturbations, ranking of train–test gaps, and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus removing random examples.

missing.what: Matched-epoch VGG11 constant-schedule comparison: batch 128, learning rate 0.001 versus batch 640, learning rate 0.005; approximately matching training and held-out curves. Also record the cyclic batch-size versus cyclic learning-rate curve comparison separately from Table 1.

ResNet56 batch 50, learning rate 0.1 versus batch 500 with several learning rates, and VGG11 batch 50, learning rate 0.001 versus batch 250 with several learning rates. Proportional scaling most closely matches small-batch learning curves under the same epoch schedules.

Fashion-MNIST validation accuracy across the learning-rate and batch-size grid after 300 epochs, selecting models with approximately 100% training accuracy: accuracy improves with higher ratio and is similar across batch sizes at the same ratio. Exact point values are not recoverable from the supplied text.

Accuracy breakdown under joint scaling, separated by dataset size and scaling factor. For 12,000 examples, β=1 gives 83.0±0.15%, β=11 gives 81.0±0.3%, and β=13 gives 69.3±7.83%; for 45,000 examples the corresponding values are 90.4±0.12%, 89.7±0.22%, and 89.1±0.42%. Values are maximum validation accuracy across runs, not final-epoch accuracy; β=15 includes divergence in at least one seed.

record.verdict_notes: Missing components of V1 are untested, not evidence of an incomplete effect. Figure 6 supports coexistence despite partial label corruption; it does not establish chance performance after fully random-label training. Table 1's prose says all cyclic schedules have higher loss, but discrete learning-rate loss is actually 0.054 versus the constant schedule's 0.056.

versions.untested_parts: Does not compare natural-label training directly against random-label held-out chance accuracy using the same architectures and recipes; its noisy-label experiments use 25% or 50% randomized training labels and report validation performance after fitting them.
Does not test the fixed-epoch large-batch penalty against smaller batches across image and language benchmarks, or compare the listed adaptation strategies under fixed epoch budgets.
